title: For Walmart, Replacing Humans With Robots Is a Multibillion-Dollar Struggle
source_used: Livemint, which carries the Wall Street Journal story (WSJ original returned HTTP 401)
key_facts: Walmart's decade-long effort to automate its warehouses has hit breakdowns, costly redesigns, packaging problems and trouble with oversized goods.
Walmart relies on more than 140,000 warehouse workers and is automating most of its roughly 200 US supply-chain buildings.
Rob Montgomery, head of supply-chain operations for Walmart U.S., says the company is in 'peak complexity'.
Walmart's boxes are too big for the automated systems and the small shuttle robots break down too often.
Symbotic, in which Walmart holds a 12.6% stake, supplies the systems; under 10% of its robots were being repaired at a time last year, about 5% in recent months, a Symbotic spokesman said.
Executives say fewer warehouse workers will eventually be needed but automation will not require layoffs; spending on the rollout is expected to peak this year and next.
A person familiar said monthly power bills at automated grocery sites can reach $800,000 versus about $250,000 before.
quote_evidence: “We are kind of in this peak complexity,” said Rob Montgomery, head of supply-chain operations for Walmart U.S., who is overseeing the automation transition now under way at most of Walmart’s roughly 200 U.S. supply-chain buildings.
The cardboard shipping boxes Walmart has used for years are too big for the automated systems.
The miniature robots that shuttle goods break down too often.
why_it_matters_hint: Shows how hard it is for the biggest US retailer to replace warehouse labour with robots, and what that means for its jobs and costs.
notes: WSJ original blocked (HTTP 401); text read on Livemint's syndicated copy of the WSJ story.
